title: Supersingular isogeny path finding

problem.name: Supersingular isogeny path finding
problem.statement_latex: Given supersingular elliptic curves $E,E'/\mathbb F_{p^2}$, output an explicitly evaluable isogeny $E\to E'$. One may represent it as a composition of low-degree isogenies. This is the unrestricted path problem underlying several isogeny constructions. Complexity is measured in field-operation-scale time, with polynomial-bit arithmetic translated into quantum gates and classical bit operations.
problem.statement_text: Given supersingular elliptic curves $E,E'/\mathbb F_{p^2}$, output an explicitly evaluable isogeny $E\to E'$. One may represent it as a composition of low-degree isogenies. This is the unrestricted path problem underlying several isogeny constructions. Complexity is measured in field-operation-scale time, with polynomial-bit arithmetic translated into quantum gates and classical bit operations.

quantum.details_latex: Amplitude amplification reaches the subgraph of curves defined over $\mathbb F_p$, after which the algorithm uses its abelian structure. Reversible isogeny evaluation and the endpoint-recognition predicate determine the arithmetic factors. The exponent absorbs the subexponential costs required by the second stage.

classical.headline_latex: $p^{1/3+o(1)}$ time and memory, Wesolowski supersingular isogeny algorithm.
classical.headline_text: $p^{1/3+o(1)}$ time and memory, Wesolowski supersingular isogeny algorithm.
classical.details_latex: The result uses a heuristic assumption on smoothness of the relevant random integers. Non-scalar endomorphism computations and reductions between endomorphism and isogeny problems produce an explicitly evaluable path. The $o(1)$ exponent includes superpolynomial factors in $\log p$. For regimes using the random-walk approach, Delfs--Galbraith provides a $p^{1/2+o(1)}$ alternative with different memory requirements.

strength.description_latex: Polynomial speedup through a smaller exponential constant in the input bit length $\log p$, from $1/3$ to $1/4$. Amplitude amplification is an essential quantum component.
strength.description_text: Polynomial speedup through a smaller exponential constant in the input bit length $\log p$, from $1/3$ to $1/4$. Amplitude amplification is an essential quantum component.

evidence.description_latex: Partial evidence for explicit curves. The classical $p^{1/3+o(1)}$ comparison is a 2026 preprint with a stated smoothness heuristic.

hardware.description_latex: Curve registers have polynomial size in $\log p$. Reversible field arithmetic and exponentially many coherent operations require fault tolerance; runtime is the principal obstacle at cryptographic sizes.
